questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: An animal in which any plane passing through the central axis of the body divides it into two identical halves shows radial symmetry. Which of the following groups shows this body plan?

solution.explanation: NCERT: when any plane passing through the central axis divides the organism into two identical halves, it is radial symmetry. Coelenterates, ctenophores and (adult) echinoderms have this body plan. Annelids, arthropods and flatworms are bilaterally symmetrical: only one plane gives identical left and right halves.
steps: Radial symmetry → coelenterates, ctenophores, adult echinoderms
Bilateral symmetry → annelids, arthropods, flatworms and others
solution.why_others_wrong: Annelids, arthropods and flatworms can be divided into identical halves along one plane only (bilateral symmetry).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Animal Kingdom', basis of classification: symmetry
solution.final_answer: Option C: Coelenterates

R: optimum temperature and pH → true
General property ≠ cause of thermal stability → R does not explain A

Which of the following statements about proteins are correct?

solution.explanation: Proteins are linear chains of amino acids, i.e. heteropolymers. The first amino acid of a chain is the N-terminal amino acid and the last is the C-terminal. questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: As substrate concentration is raised, the velocity of an enzyme-catalysed reaction rises at first and then reaches a maximum (Vmax) that is not exceeded by any further rise in substrate concentration. This is because:

The extra substrate denatures the enzyme
The extra substrate acts as a competitive inhibitor
The products formed lower the activation energy further

solution.explanation: NCERT: the velocity rises with substrate concentration and reaches Vmax, which is not exceeded, because the enzyme molecules are fewer than the substrate molecules; once they are all saturated, there are no free enzyme molecules to bind more substrate.
steps: All enzyme molecules occupied → saturation → Vmax

solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biomolecules', enzymes: factors affecting enzyme activity

Enzymes are damaged above about 40 °C → II false

R: body cannot synthesise them → true
solution.why_others_wrong: B denies the direct causal link; C and D call a true statement false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biomolecules', proteins

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: A protein is made of two polypeptide chains, one of 21 amino acids and the other of 30 amino acids. Each chain is a linear chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. How many peptide bonds are present in the protein?

solution.explanation: In a linear chain of n amino acids, n − 1 peptide bonds join neighbours. Each chain is counted separately because there is no peptide bond between the two chains.
solution.shortcut: Peptide bonds = total amino acids − number of chains = 51 − 2 = 49.
solution.why_others_wrong: 51 counts amino acids, not bonds; 50 treats both chains as one continuous chain; 48 subtracts one bond too many.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biomolecules', proteins
solution.final_answer: Option D: 49

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Which sequence correctly describes the catalytic cycle of an enzyme?

options.text: Products are released → substrate binds to the active site → bonds of the substrate are broken → enzyme alters its shape
Enzyme alters its shape → substrate binds to a site away from the active site → products are released → enzyme–product complex forms
Substrate binds to the active site → bonds of the substrate are broken → enzyme alters its shape around the products → products stay bound permanently

Substrate binds to the active site → enzyme alters its shape to fit more tightly around the substrate → bonds of the substrate are broken and an enzyme–product complex forms → products are released and the free enzyme can bind another substrate molecule

solution.explanation: NCERT gives four steps: (1) the substrate binds to the active site; (2) binding induces the enzyme to alter its shape and fit more tightly around the substrate; (3) the active site breaks the chemical bonds of the substrate and an enzyme–product complex forms; (4) the enzyme releases the products and the free enzyme is ready for another substrate molecule.
steps: Bind → induced fit → bond breaking (EP complex) → release and reuse

solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biomolecules', enzymes: nature of enzyme action

Which of the following definitions of respiratory volumes and capacities are correct?

Low pO₂, low pCO₂, lesser H⁺ concentration and higher temperature

solution.explanation: Binding of O₂ to haemoglobin depends mainly on pO₂; pCO₂, H⁺ concentration and temperature also interfere. In the alveoli there is high pO₂, low pCO₂, lesser H⁺ concentration and lower temperature, all favourable for oxyhaemoglobin formation. The opposite conditions in the tissues favour dissociation of O₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: A gives the tissue conditions, which favour dissociation; B and C mix favourable and unfavourable factors.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', transport of gases: transport of oxygen
solution.final_answer: Option D: High pO₂, low pCO₂, lesser H⁺ concentration and lower temperature

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: The partial pressures (in mm Hg) are: alveoli, pO₂ 104 and pCO₂ 40; deoxygenated blood, pO₂ 40 and pCO₂ 45; oxygenated blood, pO₂ 95 and pCO₂ 40. What are the partial-pressure gradients for O₂ from the alveoli to the deoxygenated blood reaching the lungs, and for CO₂ from that blood to the alveoli?

options.text: 55 mm Hg for O₂ and 5 mm Hg for CO₂
64 mm Hg for O₂ and 5 mm Hg for CO₂
64 mm Hg for O₂ and 45 mm Hg for CO₂
104 mm Hg for O₂ and 40 mm Hg for CO₂

solution.explanation: Gas moves down its partial-pressure gradient. Deoxygenated blood arrives at the alveoli, so the O₂ gradient is alveolar pO₂ minus blood pO₂, and the CO₂ gradient is blood pCO₂ minus alveolar pCO₂.
steps: CO₂ still diffuses readily because its solubility is 20–25 times that of O₂
solution.why_others_wrong: 55 mm Hg uses the oxygenated-blood pO₂ (95) in place of the alveolar value; 45 mm Hg is the blood pCO₂ itself, not a difference; 104 and 40 are the alveolar values, not gradients.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', exchange of gases
solution.final_answer: Option B: 64 mm Hg for O₂ and 5 mm Hg for CO₂

Alveoli: low pCO₂ → HCO₃⁻ → CO₂ + H₂O → R false

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Which sequence correctly describes normal (quiet) expiration in humans?

Diaphragm and external inter-costal muscles contract → thoracic volume increases → intra-pulmonary pressure rises above atmospheric pressure → air is expelled
Diaphragm relaxes → thoracic volume increases → intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure → air is expelled
Inter-costal muscles relax → pulmonary volume increases → intra-pulmonary pressure becomes equal to atmospheric pressure → air is expelled

Deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the cardiac cycle are correct?

(a) As the ventricles contract, ventricular pressure rises and closes the tricuspid and bicuspid valves because of the attempted backflow of blood into the atria.
(b) As ventricular pressure rises further, the semilunar valves guarding the pulmonary artery and the aorta are forced open.
(c) As the ventricles relax, ventricular pressure falls and the semilunar valves close, preventing backflow.
(d) Each ventricle pumps out about 70 mL of blood in each cardiac cycle.
(e) The atria and the ventricles contract at the same time.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

When the ventricles relax, their pressure falls and the semilunar valves close. The stroke volume is about 70 mL per ventricle per cycle. The atria contract first (atrial systole) and the ventricles afterwards, when the action potential reaches them through the AVN and bundle of His; the two do not contract together.

It contains the larger plasma proteins but no minerals
It has the same mineral distribution as plasma, while the larger proteins and most formed elements stay in the blood vessels
It is identical to plasma, including the larger proteins

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Filtrate enters the descending limb of Henle's loop at an osmolarity of 300 mOsmol L⁻¹ and reaches the hairpin bend at 1200 mOsmol L⁻¹. Assume that the amount of solute in the filtrate does not change along this limb. If 20 mL of filtrate enters the descending limb, what volume reaches the hairpin bend?

solution.concept: Concentration of the filtrate in the descending limb
solution.explanation: NCERT: the descending limb of the loop of Henle is permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes, so the filtrate gets concentrated as it moves down by losing water, while its solutes stay in it. With the solute amount fixed, volume × osmolarity stays constant, so a four-fold rise in osmolarity means the volume falls to one-fourth.

solution.why_others_wrong: 80 mL multiplies by the ratio instead of dividing; 15 mL is the volume of water lost, not the volume left; 20 mL assumes the filtrate is concentrated by gaining solutes, but this limb is almost impermeable to electrolytes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Excretory Products and their Elimination', urine formation: function of the tubules (Henle's loop) and mechanism of concentration of the filtrate
solution.final_answer: Option D: 5 mL

questions.question_text: Apart from increasing water reabsorption from the latter parts of the tubule, ADH can also increase the glomerular filtration rate. It does so by:

Constricting blood vessels, which raises blood pressure and thereby glomerular blood flow

questions.question_text: Site A on an axon has just been stimulated, and site B, immediately ahead of it, is still at rest. Which statement about the charges and the local current between the two sites is correct?

options.text: At A the inner surface is negative and at B it is positive; current flows on the inner surface from B to A
At A the inner surface is positive and at B it is negative; current flows on the inner surface from A to B and on the outer surface from B to A
At A the inner surface is positive and at B it is negative; current flows on both the inner and the outer surface from A to B
At A and at B the inner surface is positive; no current flows between them

solution.explanation: At the stimulated site A, Na⁺ influx reverses the polarity: the outer surface becomes negative and the inner surface positive. At site B, still at rest, the outer surface is positive and the inner negative. So current flows on the inner surface from A to B, and on the outer surface from B to A, completing the circuit. This depolarises B, and the impulse moves along the axon.
steps: Inner current A → B; outer current B → A
solution.why_others_wrong: A reverses the charges; C ignores that the circuit is completed in the opposite direction on the outer surface; D treats the resting site as depolarised.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Neural Control and Coordination', generation and conduction of nerve impulse
solution.final_answer: Option B: At A the inner surface is positive and at B it is negative; current flows on the inner surface from A to B and on the outer surface from B to A
